Henri Matisse. The French painter, sculptor, and printmaker lived from eighteen sixty-nine to nineteen fifty-four. His radical use of colour, expressive line, and simplified form made him one of the twentieth century's most influential artists. A founder of Fauvism and a lifelong innovator, Matisse pursued beauty and joy through paint, pushing abstraction toward pure expression. His late paper cut-outs represent one of art history's most inventive reinventions, proving that an aging master could pioneer new aesthetic territory.

Matisse was born in Le Cateau-Cambrésis in eighteen sixty-nine. He studied in Paris initially under conservative classical traditions before his radical embrace of pure colour liberated modern art. He co-founded Fauvism around nineteen oh five, unleashing unnaturalistic, emotionally expressive colour applied boldly and directly. This caused scandal and outrage at the nineteen oh five Salon d'Automne.

His philosophy was revolutionary: colour is not descriptive or representational but inherently emotive. A vivid red expresses more truth about reality than a naturalistic flesh tone. He created works across diverse media: paintings, sculptures, prints, illustrated books, murals, and in his final years in the nineteen fifties, monumental paper cut-outs combining colour, form, and spiritual transcendence.

His late masterworks include Jazz from nineteen forty-seven, a book illustrated with hand-cut and hand-painted coloured papers combining text and image. He also created chapel designs at Vence from nineteen forty-nine to nineteen fifty-one, synthesizing architecture, stained glass, and decoration. He maintained a lifelong productive artistic dialogue with Picasso, each representing contrasting yet complementary modernist paths: Matisse with colour and decorative harmony versus Picasso's form and cubist fragmentation.

He achieved international celebrity and major retrospectives by the nineteen thirties and remained creatively experimental throughout his eighties, proving that aging artists could pioneer entirely new aesthetic territories. His philosophy that joy and beauty were valid artistic goals, against modernist severity, profoundly influenced postwar art, abstract expressionism, and contemporary approaches to colour and form. His late cut-outs proved that radical innovation and artistic reinvention were possible at any age, simplifying form to its essential elements while amplifying colour's spiritual power. Matisse remains an enduring model of artistic freedom: a master who transcended tradition, reinvented himself repeatedly, and demonstrated that pleasure and profundity are not mutually exclusive in art.
